entities.name: Ghana National Mosque
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The National Mosque of Ghana in Accra, officially opened in 2004 — built with funding from the Islamic Development Bank and designed to accommodate 15,000 worshippers, with a capacity for an additional 20,000 in its courtyard — is one of West Africa's largest mosques and a symbol of Ghana's growing Muslim community (approximately 18-20% of Ghana's 32 million people) and of the strengthening ties between Ghana and the broader Islamic world, particularly the Gulf states and the OIC.

Ghana's Muslim community has deep historical roots: Islam entered the region that is now northern Ghana via trans-Saharan trade routes from the 14th-15th centuries, and the northern regions of Ghana (Upper East, Upper West, Northern) have Muslim majorities. The National Mosque in Accra represents the emergence of this historically northern Ghanaian Muslim tradition into the capital's public life and national symbolism.

The mosque's construction, funded by the Islamic Development Bank (IDB) with additional support from Muslim-majority states, is part of a broader pattern of Gulf-funded mosque construction across sub-Saharan Africa that has both strengthened Muslim communities' physical infrastructure and raised questions about the spread of more conservative Wahhabi/Salafi Islamic practices alongside the financial support. Ghana's tradition of religious tolerance (Christianity and Islam have coexisted peacefully) makes the National Mosque a symbol of Ghana's pluralistic religious landscape.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ghana's National Mosque — representing the national presence of Ghana's historically rooted Muslim community, funded by Islamic Development Bank as part of Gulf soft power in Africa, and a symbol of Ghana's religious pluralism — reflects the growing prominence of Islam in West African national life.
